messages.mes:
The road took him down between hedged fields toward the eastern gate, where a trickle of carts and foot traffic funneled past a squat stone tower. Two guards in patched brigandines watched the line, waving through most and questioning a badger-faced carter about his cargo. One of them gave Alaric's sword and armor a glance—nothing more than a blink of assessment, the kind paid to any armed traveler—before motioning him on with the rest.

Inside the walls, Ashbridge smelled of bread and horse dung and woodsmoke. Timber-framed houses leaned over cobbled streets; a smith's hammer rang somewhere to the left; a woman argued with a fishmonger about the freshness of a pike. People were busy with their mornings and had no interest in him. He asked his way once at a well, and a girl with yokes on both shoulders jerked her chin up a lane: "Guild's the stone one with the blue door, can't miss it."

He couldn't. The hall stood where two streets crossed, wide-fronted, its lintel carved with crossed swords and a stag. Through the open door came the clack of a wooden marker on a board and the low murmur of men and women in leather and mail. A one-armed man sat on a bench outside sharpening a knife against a whetstone, unhurried, not looking up.

Inside, morning light fell through high windows onto a long counter, behind which a broad woman with grey-shot braids was sorting contract slips into a rack. To the left, a large board stood thick with posted work. To the right, a smaller desk held a ledger, an inkwell, and a brass plate engraved with the word REGISTRATION.

The woman at the counter looked up as he approached. "Morning. Fresh face or old business?"

"Fresh face, then." She set down the rack of slips and slid a ledger across the counter, its pages ruled in close columns. "Registration's a one-time fee. Two silver. That puts you on the rolls, gets you a member's mark, and lets you take contracts off that board there—Novice work to start, nothing above what your strength can carry."

She tapped a smudge of ink in the ledger's margin. "The Guild measures what you are, but it doesn't make it. Power rank's a separate thing—the stone'll read you when we do the measuring, and whatever it says is what the contracts will take you for. Guild rank's just standing with us. One climbs by turning in honest work."

She turned the ledger to face him and set a stub of pencil beside it. "Name as you want it written, that's all the paperwork there is. Two silver at the desk and we'll do the measuring stone."

Behind him, someone laughed at the board and wrenched a slip free; the door let in a draught that smelled of the street. The woman waited, hands resting flat on the counter, in no hurry at all.

messages.mes:
He wrote the name and pushed the coins across. She swept them into a drawer, checked the ledger's line, and nodded once, as if filing him somewhere in her head alongside the ink.

"Alaric. Right." From under the counter she lifted a flat wooden case, opened it, and took out a small disc of pale metal, stamped with the Guild's crossed swords and stag. "Member's plate. Keep it on you—merchants, gate guards, other branches, they'll know what it means. Lose it and it costs to replace, so don't."

She set it in his palm, then turned and thumped a fist on the counter's far end. "Marta. Stone."

A younger woman with ink-stained fingers came out of a back room wiping them on her apron, followed by a second carrying something like a short pillar of cloudy crystal on a cloth-wrapped board. They set it on the counter between Alaric and the racks of slips. The crystal caught the window light and held it, dull and faintly green.

"Hand flat on the stone," the counter woman said. "Doesn't hurt, doesn't bite. It reads what you've got and no more. Power rank's a separate scale from ours—it says what you are, not who you work for. Whatever it shows, that's the rank the contracts will take you for."

She stood back, arms folded. Behind him the board-clatter went on; nobody else in the hall seemed to spare the ceremony a glance, which suggested it happened often enough to bore them.

"Whenever you're ready."

The crystal was cool under his palm, cooler than the room, and for a moment nothing happened at all. Then a pale glow woke inside it, gathering toward the center like fog closing around a lantern. It steadied at a faint green, dim and even, and letters surfaced in the haze—shallow, as if cut in ice.

*Level 1. Rank F.*

Marta leaned in, read it, and wrote something small in a side ledger with her ink-stained pencil. "F," she said. "Base stage." No surprise in it; most hands that touched the stone on their first day came out the same.

The counter woman unfolded her arms. "There it is, then. F-rank, Novice standing—nothing to be ashamed of, everybody starts there, and the ones who don't are usually lying." She plucked a chalk stub from a cup and marked something on the member's rack where the ledger line sat. "F work's posted on the low end of the board. Escort's legs, culling vermin, deliveries into the country. Pay's modest but it's honest, and turning them in clean is how you climb."

She slid the crystal's cloth-wrapped board aside and rested a hand on the rack of contract slips. "Board's there if you want work today. Or you take the lay of the town first, come back when you're ready—the board doesn't care which."

Behind him, the one-armed man from the bench shuffled in and queued a few paces back, whetstone still scraping lazily against steel.

messages.mes:
The north gate stood open to the morning traffic, and the gatewarden on the arch gave Alaric's sword a glance and nothing more. Beyond the walls the road dropped through goat pens and garden plots, then shook off the outskirts and ran east between hedgerows gone straggly and wild.

The old quarry track was impossible to lose. Ruts from fifty years of stone-carts had hardened into the earth like fossilized waves, and his boots followed them without asking. Early on there were others: a drover with geese, a haywain loaded to its side-rails, two Guild men riding west with mud to their knees. By the time the sun stood overhead the road had emptied, and the only company was the tick of heat out of the scrub and a crow that followed him fence-post to fence-post for a mile, hoping he was the dying sort.

The leaning boundary stone rose out of the heather where the sketch had promised, tilted south, a chisel-cut quarry mark on its face. Up the branch track beyond it came the work of the quarry itself—iron ringing on stone, a pony stamping, a man's voice flattened by distance. Two barrowmen paused to watch him pass the junction. He kept to the main track, and the sounds fell behind.

The hill announced itself before it appeared: a greenness ahead where the moor should have been brown. Then the whole of it, a long hump grown moss-thick on its north face, dark green and wet-looking, exactly the rug the counter woman had promised. The track ran to its foot and stopped.

The crack faced the track, two men wide, and the moss stopped at its edges clean as a shaved jaw. A short grey stake stood beside the mouth with the Guild's brand burned into it, weathered to illegibility. A path of trampled dirt led the last few yards, littered with split barrel staves and a scatter of small bones gone chalk-white.

From inside came a smell—woodsmoke, wet animal—and beneath it, far down, a slow drip of water.

messages.mes:
The crack narrowed two steps in and then opened out, and the reason for the Guild's stake became plain: a crude palisade of sharpened logs crossed the passage, lashed with cord, a gate of crossbars set into its middle. Behind it, in a niche cut into the rock, sat a grey-bearded man on a three-legged stool with a ledger open on his knees and a tallow lamp at his elbow.

"Name and branch," he said, before Alaric was even through the mouth. He didn't get up. The light from outside caught the ledger's columns—dates, names, times in, times out, some of the last column empty.

He took Alaric's slip, read the seal, and copied the name onto a line with a stub of charcoal. "Eighth slot's free. You're the only one in today, so the cap's no trouble." He handed the slip back and unhooked the crossbars one by one, each off its peg with the care of habit. "First level's the warrens' upper diggings—scouts mostly, warriors if you push toward the down-slopes. Anything talks to you, that's deeper than your contract. Kill it or back out, either's your affair." The last bar came free and he dragged the gate open. "Ledger rule: dead men get their line struck through. Don't make me ink one."

Past the palisade the tunnel was a goblin hole, not a mine: walls grubbed and pocked, roots from the moss above hanging through the ceiling like wet hair, a smoke-blackened alcove with old fire-scarred stones. It sloped down by degrees, breathing that woodsmoke-and-wet-animal smell out of the dark. The floor was tracked with footprints, barefoot, all sizes small.

The passage forked, and a broken arrow shaft kicked into the wall by his boot pointed—deliberately or not—down the left branch. The right branch was quieter, darker, and drifted colder air.

He took the passage forward, and the dark thickened until the entrance was a grey coin far behind. Then, ahead around a bulge of rock, a sound: a chittering, high and conversational, two voices maybe three, and a thin rattle that might have been bone on stone.

The bulge curved away and he rounded it, and there they were. Three goblins in the tunnel beyond, squat and grey-green, gathered around a firepit in a widened hollow—a scout's watchpost. One turned a spit of something over the coals. One sat picking its teeth with a fishbone. The third was shaking a pouch of small bones against its ear, and it was the third that saw him first.

The rattle stopped. The goblin's ears went up, and it shrieked—one short, flat bark—and all three came off their marks, the tooth-picker snatching up a short crooked blade from beside the fire, the spit-turner kicking its pit over in a spray of embers as it grabbed a spear.

The bone-shaker's bark still hung in the tunnel air when Alaric's blade came up, edge forward, weight settled back onto his rear foot. Guard.

The three goblins did not rush him. That was the first thing the warrens taught: these were scouts, and scouts looked before they leapt. They spread along the hollow in a loose crescent, the spear-carrier in the middle, and came on at a quick, hunched shuffle, feet finding the torn floor without a sound. The tooth-picker circled wide, angling along the tunnel wall where the roots hung thickest, its crooked blade held low and reversed. The one with the bone pouch stayed by the dead fire, rattling it once, twice—a signal, quick and sharp, thrown down the down-sloping dark of the tunnel behind it.

Something answered from below. A deeper voice, two barks, and then the flat slap of bare feet starting up the slope.

The spear goblin closed the last of the distance in a rush, and it did not use the spear. It swung the butt of it like a club, a short hooked strike that came under Alaric's raised guard and cracked against his jaw, snapping his head sideways. Fire ran along his cheekbone; his mouth filled with the copper taste of a bitten tongue.

The one with the crooked blade had been moving the whole time. It slipped along the wall of roots and came in fast from his left, low, and its blade wanted his hip—but the guard was up now, boots planted, blade angled to cover, and the goblin's strike met steel instead of flesh. It skidded along the flat of his longsword with a shriek of metal and glanced into his side, more punch than cut, a bruising weight that drove the breath short.

The spear goblin came again before he could reset, and its strike landed on his shoulder, hard, knocking the arm half-numb down to the fingers.

The tunnel rang with their movement and his own boots scraping for purchase. Behind them, at the dead fire, the bone-pouch goblin stayed where it was, rattling its bones in a slow, delighted shake, watching. From below, the heavy feet were closer.

Alaric's blade held its line, guard high, his jaw throbbing and his shoulder burning, and both goblins crouched a pace off, ready to come in again.

The swing had spent Alaric's whole body to make it, and the tooth-picker was inside the finished arc before he could bring the blade back. No crooked steel this time: it turned a heel-kick into the meat of his thigh, a short ugly strike that numbed the leg from hip to knee and put a wobble in his stance.

Then the wounded one came off the wall. It ducked under his shoulder and drove its skull up into his chest, bone meeting breastbone with a knock he felt in his back teeth, folding him around the blow.

The tooth-picker slid back a step, light on its feet, untouched. The spear goblin stood its ground a pace off, breathing wet, red running off its fingertips.

Two steps was all the tunnel gave him. The goblins had been circling on either side for exactly this, and the moment his back was turned they were on him—the crooked blade's edge already swinging as he broke from the guard, a backhand cut across his shoulder blades that laid him open to the spine. The longsword lay in the muck a hand's width from his open fingers. The two scouts bent over him, chittering, already tugging at the straps of his armor.
